lines.text: Your bank doesn't know your password. And that's exactly why you're safe.
You'd think they keep it in a file somewhere, and check it when you log in. They don't.
Instead, your password goes into a math blender called a hash. Out comes a long scramble of letters and numbers.
Same password in, same scramble out. Every single time. Change one letter, and the whole thing changes.
And here's the trick: it only works one way. You can't un-blend a smoothie back into fruit.
So when you log in, they blend what you typed, and compare the scrambles. Match? You're in. They never needed the real thing.
Smart sites also add salt: a random pinch mixed into every password, so two people with the same password still get different scrambles.
So how do passwords still leak? When a list of scrambles gets stolen, thieves can't reverse them. They guess.
They blend millions of common passwords, like one two three four five six, and look for a match.
That's why good sites use a slow blender on purpose. One login takes a blink. A million guesses take forever.
And that's how Orbi Transfer protects your files. Your passcode never even leaves your phone.
Your phone blends it three hundred and ten thousand times. The server keeps only a scramble of a proof, so it can't open your file.
Guess wrong twelve times, and the file locks for good.
